patient.name: Kwame Mensah
patient.complaint: Black, tarry stools and one coffee-ground vomit after weeks of night-time epigastric pain
background: Scaffolder in Lewisham with chronic low back pain
Buys ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day over the counter
Smokes 15 a day; drinks 20 units a week

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with epigastric pain related to food, NSAID use or H. pylori, and complications: coffee-ground vomit and melaena (bleeding) or sudden severe pain with a rigid abdomen and air under the diaphragm (perforation).

points: Kwame, 46, has had **epigastric pain** for 6 weeks.
It **wakes him at night** and is **eased by eating** or milk.
Today: black, sticky, foul stools and one **coffee-ground** vomit.

visual.title: Where Kwame's pain is
visual.caption: Epigastric pain and tenderness: the territory of peptic ulcer disease and gastritis.

steps.lead: Kwame has the two big causes in one man: **NSAIDs** and possibly **H. pylori**, both breaking down the mucosal barrier.

steps.q: Kwame's pain is worse at night and relieved by food. Which ulcer fits best?
steps.r: **Duodenal** ulcer pain is relieved by eating and worse when the stomach is empty or at night. **Gastric** ulcer pain is worsened by eating.

steps.lead: Kwame's food-relieved night pain points to a **duodenal** ulcer, 4 times commoner than gastric and usually **H. pylori**.
Always take a drug history: Kwame's **ibuprofen** is the culprit to stop. Also ask about aspirin, steroids, bisphosphonates and SSRIs.
Kwame is **bleeding**: coffee-ground vomit, melaena and tachycardia. A posterior duodenal ulcer can erode the **gastroduodenal artery**.

steps.text: Sudden severe pain, a **rigid** abdomen and guarding means **perforation**, not just a bleed. Kwame's soft abdomen argues against it, but always check.
Gastritis gives the same dyspepsia and causes but **no ulcer** at endoscopy; it is inflammation only.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?': urea breath test or stool antigen for H. pylori in uncomplicated dyspepsia, urgent 2-week-wait OGD for age 55 or over with weight loss, OGD for a bleed, and erect chest X-ray for suspected perforation.

steps.title: Kwame's bloods in ED
steps.text: A **raised urea with normal creatinine** suggests an upper GI bleed: digested blood is a protein load.

visual.title: Kwame's haemoglobin
visual.caption: Falling Hb before endoscopy, recovering once the bleeding ulcer is treated and blood is given.

steps.q: Kwame has an upper GI bleed. Which investigation confirms the cause?
steps.r: **OGD** finds and treats the bleeding ulcer and allows biopsy. A breath test only shows H. pylori.

points: OGD: **posterior duodenal ulcer** with a visible vessel.
Biopsy rapid urease test: **H. pylori positive**.

steps.lead: OGD was Kwame's **gold standard**: it confirmed the bleeding ulcer. If an ulcer needs checking for healing, repeat endoscopy at **6 to 8 weeks**.
Without a bleed, Kwame's GP would have started with a **urea breath test** or **stool antigen**, not serology. At 46 without alarm features, no 2-week wait was needed.

visual.title: Age and the 2-week-wait OGD
bands: Test and treat H. pylori if no alarm features
55+ with weight loss and dyspepsia: 2WW OGD
visual.label: Kwame 46
visual.caption: Age 55 or over with weight loss plus dyspepsia, or alarm features at any age (anaemia, vomiting, dysphagia), means urgent OGD.

steps.lead: Had Kwame been over 55 with **treatment-resistant** dyspepsia but no 2WW features, he would get a **non-urgent** endoscopy.
Kwame has no peritonism. If he had, an **erect chest X-ray** looking for **free air under the diaphragm** comes first.

steps.text: H. pylori **serology** stays positive after eradication, so it cannot confirm cure. Use the **urea breath test** or **stool antigen**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': stop the NSAID, PPI for H. pylori-negative ulcers, 7 days of triple therapy for H. pylori-positive ones, and for perforation IV fluids and group and save before laparotomy.

steps.lead: Kwame's bleed meant **urgent hospital admission**. A perforated ulcer would need **IV fluids and group and save**, then **laparotomy**.

steps.title: Kwame's bleed, step by step
nodes: ABCDE: two large-bore cannulas, bloods, group and save or crossmatch
Urgent OGD: find and treat the bleeding ulcer
Treat the cause: H. pylori eradication or PPI

steps.q: Kwame's ulcer is H. pylori positive and he has no allergies. Which treatment eradicates it?
o: Omeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin for 7 days
steps.r: **Triple therapy for 7 days**: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin (or metronidazole). PPI alone heals but does not eradicate.

steps.lead: Kwame **stops ibuprofen**, cuts down smoking and alcohol, and starts **7-day triple therapy**. Penicillin-allergic patients get PPI + clarithromycin + metronidazole.

steps.title: What to give, by H. pylori status
head: Situation
Treatment
rows: **7 days**: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin or metronidazole
Repeat, **swapping** the antibiotic not used; or bismuth quadruple therapy

steps.lead: If Kwame's eradication fails, repeat triple therapy **swapping** clarithromycin for metronidazole, or use **bismuth quadruple** therapy.
Kwame's plan follows **NICE** dyspepsia and H. pylori guidance; older patients with weight loss go via the **2-week wait** pathway.

steps.text: Retest for H. pylori after eradication with a **urea breath test**, at least 4 weeks after antibiotics and 2 weeks after stopping the PPI.
In a perforation question, the **immediate** step is resuscitation (**IV fluids**, group and save), not an OGD: endoscopy insufflates air into a hole.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: how H. pylori survives acid (urease, the basis of the breath test), how NSAIDs cause ulcers (COX-1, prostaglandins) and which artery bleeds from a posterior duodenal ulcer.

steps.lead: Kwame's **H. pylori** makes **urease**, turning urea into ammonia to neutralise acid around itself, which is why his breath test would be positive.

steps.title: Urea breath test
nodes: Labelled CO2 absorbed and breathed out

steps.lead: Kwame's ibuprofen blocks **COX-1**, cutting the **prostaglandins** that keep mucosal blood flow, mucus and bicarbonate going.

steps.title: How an NSAID makes an ulcer
nodes: Less mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow

steps.lead: Kwame's **duodenal** ulcer reflects **too much acid**; gastric ulcers more often reflect **weak mucosal defence**.

steps.q: Kwame's ulcer is on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum. Which artery is most at risk?
steps.r: The **gastroduodenal artery** runs behind the first part of the duodenum. The left gastric is the risk for lesser-curve gastric ulcers.

steps.lead: Kwame's ulcer eroded towards the **gastroduodenal artery**. A perforation would spill contents into the peritoneum: chemical, then bacterial, **peritonitis**.

mcq.q: What are the two most common causes of peptic ulcer disease?
mcq.r: **H. pylori** and **NSAIDs** both damage the mucosal barrier.

mcq.q: Which ulcer's pain is typically relieved by eating?
mcq.r: **Duodenal** pain eases with food and is worse at night; gastric pain is worse with food.

mcq.q: Which type of peptic ulcer is more likely to be malignant?
mcq.r: **Gastric** ulcers are more often malignant, so they are biopsied and rechecked.

mcq.q: Which artery is most commonly implicated in a bleeding duodenal ulcer?
mcq.r: The **gastroduodenal artery** lies behind the posterior duodenal wall.

mcq.q: Which tests are preferred for H. pylori?
o: Urea breath test or stool antigen
mcq.r: **Urea breath test** or **stool antigen**; serology cannot show cure.

mcq.q: What does an erect chest X-ray show in a perforated ulcer?
How long is H. pylori triple therapy given?
mcq.r: **7 days**: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin or metronidazole.

mcq.q: What is the eradication regimen for a penicillin-allergic patient?
What is the definitive management of a perforated peptic ulcer?
mcq.r: Stabilise with IV fluids and group and save, then **laparotomy**.

mcq.q: Which enzyme lets H. pylori survive gastric acid?
mcq.r: **Urease** makes ammonia, neutralising acid locally; the basis of the breath test.

glossary.PUD: Peptic ulcer disease: ulceration of the stomach or duodenal lining.
glossary.peptic ulcer: A break in the gastric or duodenal lining caused by acid and pepsin.
glossary.gastritis: Inflammation of the stomach lining without ulceration.
glossary.duodenal ulcer: Ulcer in the first part of the duodenum; pain eased by eating.
glossary.gastric ulcer: Ulcer in the stomach; pain worsened by eating and more often malignant.
glossary.H. pylori: Helicobacter pylori: a Gram-negative, urease-producing bacterium that colonises the gastric antrum.
glossary.NSAIDs: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen, which block COX enzymes.
glossary.COX-1: Cyclo-oxygenase 1: makes the prostaglandins that protect the gastric mucosa.
glossary.prostaglandins: Lipid messengers that keep gastric mucus, bicarbonate and blood flow going.
glossary.urease: Enzyme that splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide.
glossary.urea breath test: Swallowed labelled urea is split by H. pylori; labelled CO2 in breath shows active infection.
glossary.stool antigen test: Detects H. pylori proteins in faeces; shows active infection.
glossary.serology: Blood antibody test; stays positive after H. pylori is cured.
glossary.dyspepsia: Upper abdominal discomfort or indigestion, often after eating.
glossary.epigastric: The upper central abdomen, just below the sternum.
glossary.melaena: Black, tarry, foul-smelling stool from digested blood in an upper GI bleed.
glossary.coffee-ground: Vomit containing dark altered blood that looks like coffee grounds.
glossary.perforation: A hole through the full thickness of the gut wall.
glossary.peritonism: Signs of peritoneal irritation: guarding, rebound tenderness and a rigid abdomen.
glossary.peritonitis: Inflammation of the peritoneum, here from spilled gastric contents.
glossary.rebound tenderness: Pain worse when pressure is suddenly released; a sign of peritonitis.
glossary.guarding: Involuntary tensing of the abdominal muscles over an inflamed area.
glossary.gastroduodenal artery: Branch of the common hepatic artery behind the first part of the duodenum.
glossary.left gastric artery: Coeliac trunk branch along the lesser curve; bleeds from gastric ulcers.
glossary.OGD: Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy: camera examination of the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum.
glossary.PPI: Proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole; blocks parietal cell acid secretion.
glossary.triple therapy: PPI plus two antibiotics for 7 days to eradicate H. pylori.
glossary.quadruple therapy: Bismuth-based regimen of PPI, bismuth and two antibiotics for resistant H. pylori.
glossary.clarithromycin: Macrolide antibiotic used in H. pylori triple therapy.
glossary.metronidazole: Antibiotic used in H. pylori eradication, especially with penicillin allergy.
glossary.laparotomy: Open surgery through a large abdominal incision.
glossary.group and save: Blood test of blood group and antibody screen so blood can be issued quickly.
glossary.2-week wait: NHS urgent suspected cancer referral: seen or tested within two weeks.
glossary.bisphosphonates: Osteoporosis drugs such as risedronate that can irritate the upper GI mucosa.
glossary.SSRIs: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as fluoxetine; raise GI bleeding risk.
glossary.pneumoperitoneum: Free air in the peritoneal cavity, usually from a perforated viscus.
glossary.antrum: The lower part of the stomach before the pylorus.

practice.stem: A 61 year old woman has a 3 month history of epigastric pain that is worse after eating. She has lost 5 kg because she is afraid to eat. She takes ibuprofen for osteoarthritis. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. There is epigastric tenderness.

Chronic pancreatitis gives back pain, steatorrhoea and diabetes, usually with alcohol.

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman had 7 days of omeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin for an H. pylori-positive duodenal ulcer. Eight weeks later her symptoms persist and a urea breath test is still positive. She has no allergies.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
o: Omeprazole, amoxicillin and metronidazole for 7 days
Repeat the same regimen for 14 days
practice.e: After failed eradication, repeat triple therapy swapping the antibiotic not used: here clarithromycin for metronidazole. Bismuth quadruple therapy is the alternative.

practice.stem: A 36 year old man has a urea breath test for dyspepsia. He drinks a solution containing carbon-labelled urea, and 30 minutes later labelled carbon dioxide is detected in his breath.
practice.q: Which property of the organism explains the positive result?
practice.e: H. pylori urease splits labelled urea into ammonia and labelled CO2, which is breathed out. Urease also lets it survive gastric acid.

steps.x: A mechanism question about the test.

clues: labelled carbon dioxide is detected in his breath
steps.x: Urea split into CO2.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urease** of H. pylori.

elim: H. pylori is catalase positive, but catalase does not split urea.
Flagella help it reach the mucus layer, not make CO2.
LPS does not metabolise urea.
H. pylori does not form spores.

steps.x: **E. Urease production.**
